title: Tianhuang's Essential Dharma Gate
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up story 106 from Dogen's collection, "Tianhuang's Essential Dharma Gate," in which the rice-cake seller Long Tan becomes Tianhuang's attendant and learns that the teaching has been in the bowing, standing, and tea all along. Norman opens by grieving the police killing of Rayshard Brooks, then argues that practice is mostly hanging around together, since any moment of encounter can change us. Norman tells of missing Norman's own enlightenment when a bowl fell in the room Norman had just left, and of the Hasidic rabbi who only wanted to watch his teacher tie his shoes. Norman closes by dedicating the sesshin to racial justice.

sentences.text: *...is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas, having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept.
I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Morning, everybody.
Before I begin my talk this morning, let's take a few moments of breathing to be mindful of and grieve over another death that happened on Friday night.
Another young black man shot dead by police in Atlanta, Georgia.

His name was Rayshard Brooks, and I don't think it's a complicated incident involving a taser and some kind of scuffle at a Wendy's restaurant, but in the end it was another killing that should not have happened.
The officer who shot Rayshard was immediately fired.
I think he was charged with a crime.

Within 24 hours of the shooting, the police chief of Atlanta resigned, and an African American person was brought in to replace her, at least temporarily, and of course there were strong protests in the streets.
But the main thing is that someone has died needlessly, so let's just take a few breaths to be mindful of that and take in our feelings.
Maybe say a prayer for his well-being as he passes over, and for the well-being and condolences to his family.
This morning I have another story from Dogen's collection of stories.
This is story number 106, Tianhuang's essential dharma gate.
*Long Tan made rice cakes for a living, but when he met Tianhuang, he bowed in recognition and he left his household.*
In other words, he left his business of selling rice cakes and joined the monastery.
*Tianhuang said, "Be my attendant from now on.
I will teach you the essential dharma gate."
A year passed, and Long Tan said to him, "When I arrived, you said you would teach me the essential dharma gate, but I haven't received any instructions yet."
Tianhuang said, "I have been teaching you for a long time."
Long Tan said, "What have you been teaching me?"
Tianhuang said, "When you greet me, I bow.
When I sit, you stand next to me.
When you bring tea, I receive it from you."
Long Tan was silent.
Tianhuang said, "When you see it, you just see it.
When you think about it, you miss it."
And at that, Long Tan had great enlightenment.*
It's a lovely story, and it speaks to the radical simplicity of our practice.
There's not that much to it.
I always say it's embarrassing to spend one's life on something with so little to it as this.
There's no special insight, or powerful experience, or secret knowledge.
It's almost like there's nothing to it at all.
And there really is nothing to it at all.
And yet, I think probably most of us would agree, we're not entirely wasting our time here, because somehow we feel a virtue in it.
Somehow we do feel that practice inspires and illuminates our life, even though we can hardly tell what it is we're doing, or what it's all about.

We do seem, little by little, to be living within a different framework, I hope, with more openness, with more ease, I hope also with a little more kindness than we had before, maybe a little bit more wisdom.
So practice does somehow season us and mature us.
Or maybe it's more accurate to say that over the years of practice, we become more seasoned and more mature.
And maybe it isn't even the practice that does this.
Maybe it's just life that does it.
It's not the practice that does it, right?
We live and life changes us.
Nature takes its course.
We grow as human beings.
Maybe the point is that in ordinary conditions, nature doesn't necessarily take its course.
Maybe we don't necessarily grow up.
Practice maybe helps us to allow nature to take its course.
So in other words, what I'm saying is, there's not a skill here, or a body of knowledge.
And when you think about it, it also is not a matter of experience.
In other words, it's not a matter of gaining experience in the practice, or of having an experience or set of experiences through the practice.
It's just that time passes, we continue to practice, and our lives are as they are.
They become what they become.
They become what they become, and that's enough.
I think we do pick up over the course of time a particular feeling for life, a kind of poignant flavor in our living.
Maybe you could attribute it to Zen practice or call it Zen, but I wouldn't call it that.
I don't even know what that word Zen means anymore.
It's almost like becoming some kind of oddball word that I don't even understand.
We don't need an extra word, right?
This is just our life.
We don't need to call it this or that.
We don't need a label for it.
So here we are this week practicing a lot of zazen.
We certainly talk about zazen enough and we do it enough, but that's not really the main thing.
If you read this story, it's telling us that the main thing is just hanging around together.

That's the key point, and it's so easy to forget or miss it in the context of the lives that we're living in these times, even before the COVID times, which prevented us from hanging around together at all.
Even before that, we didn't hang around together all that much, and practice for a lot of us tends to be seen, at least at first, under the banner of personal development or individual achievement.

We begin with understanding the practice in those terms, as a kind of format for self-development or self-realization, as a kind of skill or technique or system of understanding that we could apply ourselves to and figure out and get good at, the same way that we've applied ourselves to and figured out everything else in our lives almost now, including our relationships, which we can read books about and figure out how to do.
Not really, but we can get ourselves to think that we are.
So we can look at the practice that way, but it's not like that at all.

Most of us now who practice Zen, it's very unusual really in the history of Zen, most people now in the Western world practicing Zen don't live together, as so many of the ancients did, and as some people do in residential Zen centers.
As you know, I lived many decades in residential Zen centers.
We lived together, we saw each other every day, we sat together every day, but the vast majority of people who are practicing Zen don't live like that in the West.
So we might imagine that for us the practice is not hanging around together, and especially now we only see each other on television.
But even before the pandemic, as I said, how often did we see each other really?
Maybe I practice with people that I see once a year.
Maybe we don't see each other too often.
Maybe if we're lucky, and if we're in Bellingham or close to a residential center where you can go regularly, you can maybe see each other once or twice a week.
But not that many people are able to see their sangha mates even that often.
And yet I think that this practice of hanging out together is actually essential.
It's the most important part.
When you think about it, how much time does it take to hang out?
It takes a second, a minute.
To encounter one another, to know one another, doesn't necessarily take a long time.
It actually does take a moment to observe and take into your heart the presence of another.
It takes a moment for that presence to go deep inside and impress us and turn our hearts.

And maybe this is where our zazen really helps a lot, because the zazen and the bowing and the bells and the robes and the han and the [unclear: "lore"] and the teachings help create a kind of non-normal, non-ordinary atmosphere in which these little moments can really go deep inside and cause us to feel something about our lives that we would not otherwise feel.
Not that these moments require zazen and all the rest of it.
These moments are available all the time.
The potential for us to have a deep and life-turning encounter exists in any moment.
The potential to have a moment of being with someone that will change us forever, it's always there.
In fact, if you think about it, and I think this is how Dogen thinks of it, you could say that that's the nature of every moment of lived time.
That every moment of lived time is an encounter that will change us forever, that will change us forever in profound ways.

Although, as we all know, sadly we don't experience every moment that way, because we're more or less thinking about something else, and so we're not really there to receive those moments of time in that way.
They go by and we've missed them.
It reminds me of an experience I had early on in my practice that I'll never forget.
It was in the days when I was like now being a hermit, although in these days I was a hermit by myself.
Now I'm a hermit with Kathy, but in those days I was a hermit by myself living off in the woods and doing a lot of zazen all alone and really intense about my practice.
One night I was sitting really intensely and then I needed a break, so I got up and made a cup of tea or something in another room.

When I went to do that, in the room where I was sitting, a bowl fell off a shelf and smashed, and I thought, damn, if I had been in the room then sitting, probably I would have become suddenly enlightened when that bowl fell off the shelf.
But wasn't that just my luck?
My enlightenment came and went, and unfortunately I was in the other room and I missed it.
Maybe I was on the toilet or something, and I missed it.
And I think that's right.
My enlightenment came and went and I missed it.
And probably this happens to us all the time.
Your enlightenment comes and goes, and whoops, I was thinking about something else.
I was busy.
I didn't notice it.
I was making tea.
I was reading on Facebook or something, and I missed my moment.
So yeah, it helps, right?
The zazen and the teachings and the rituals do help to keep us present so that we're more likely to feel those moments when they arrive.
And we will remember, more likely to be remembering more of the times, a lot of the times, that this actually is a moment of our lives in which something momentous is occurring.
For Dharma Seminar, we're reading a book by Anam Thubten, a wonderful local Bay Area Tibetan Buddhist teacher born in Tibet and from a distinguished family of Tibetan Buddhists.
His book is called *Choosing Compassion*.
And I was saying last week in the seminar, I noticed in a very off-handed way he says, Bodhi or Buddha comes from the root meaning to awaken, but awaken just means to be aware.
So awakeness is just awareness, which is really astonishing when you think about that.
Just to be aware, just to be there, even when you're miserable, even when you're unhappy, is to be Buddha.
And that's what Dogen is teaching too, right?
He's teaching that there are no special characteristics.
Buddha is like this and not like that.
No, any time we're there, no matter what's going on, even in our biggest delusion, when we're aware that our delusion is our delusion, we're Buddha.
This is a very simple and permissive, in the best sense, and profound, profound teaching that we'll never come to the end of appreciating.
But usually we're not appreciating that, because we would rather that things would be otherwise.
We're unsatisfied with our lives as they are.
It just doesn't seem like enough to us to be alive and to know we are alive.
We seem to require something more momentous than that.
Momentous.
Great word, right?
According to my dictionary, it means extremely important or crucial, especially in its effect on the future course of events.
And of course, it comes from the word moment, an instant of time, a very short instant of time that has significance, maybe ultimate significance.
Something is of moment, we say.
Something is momentous.
In Zen practice, momentous moments are moments of profound teaching, such as the ones Tianhuang mentions in our story.
Momentous moments, profound moments.
When we greet each other, we bow.
We stand and we sit in one another's warm presence.
We drink tea.
Probably some of you know the story of the Hasidic rabbi who went to visit his teacher and said, "I'm not coming to get the teachings.
I'm not coming to study the Torah.
I'm just coming to see how he ties his shoes.
I just want to be there when he ties his shoes."
So we spend time together in our sangha life.
In our case, very intense bits of time that we really appreciate because they're rare.
And that we repeat over and over again.
Over many decades, many of you that I'm talking to now, I know for a long time, and you know me for a long time, and you know each other for a long, long time.
And the way we know each other is not the usual way.
Not by exchanging views and opinions and personal histories and what we think about this or that.
We might do that too, but that's not really the important way that we know each other.
Because all that stuff isn't really who we are.
Sometimes we think it's who we are, but it isn't really who we are.
It's occasional.
All that stuff is literally occasional.
Occasions for us to be together, face to face.
In recent years, there's been lots of studies about the brain, and a lot of studies about the brain and emotions and the brain and meditation.
For some reason, funding is very attracted to these sorts of studies.
So they can put enormous amounts of money into these studies.
You've heard me complain about this before.
Why don't they put a little bit of money into a meditation center?
But no, they put a ton of money into studying whether or not meditation is any good.
But nobody can put any money into having a meditation center or anything like that.
God forbid they should support a meditation teacher.
Oh, no, no, not that.
But they can study whether or not meditation is a good idea, and wouldn't you know it?
They find out probably it's a good thing, meditation.
So they do all these studies about the brain, even though they know nothing about the brain.
They're so far from knowing anything about consciousness.
Never mind, I'm not complaining.
I'm just saying that there's a lot of studies about the brain.
And so David Brooks, you know who that is, right?
He's a columnist for the New York Times, and you see him on TV all the time.
He's a wise commentator who tells you how you can understand life in our times.
Anyway, some years ago, he wrote a book about all this called The Social Animal.
Because he finds that if he's interested in politics and society, and that's his business, he should be interested in human emotions.
Because that's very germane, right?
He's interested in human emotions.
In his book, he says that most of what goes on between us, the studies show this, is not what appears to be going on.
Most of what actually goes on between us is not intentional, and it isn't even conscious.
It's very subtle and mostly unknown to us.
It's literally momentous.
We stand in each other's presence, and we influence one another.
We drink in one another's being, and we know each other, and we influence each other in very mysterious ways.
And this is the heart of our practice.
We turn each other inside out simply by being in each other's presence.
By breathing together, by sitting together, by walking together, by standing together, by bowing together, even in this kind of a format, we do all these things together.
Even though now it's so odd, we're so far apart, and yet we're together.
And maybe that's why this is my subject today, exactly because we're not together.
Maybe that's why I'm talking about this.
We are each of us in our own places, miles apart from one another.
Seeing images of one another makes us perhaps recall, with great appreciation, as I am recalling now as I'm looking at the screen.
Maybe you're looking at the screen and you're only seeing me.
You don't have to, by the way.
I think you can do what I've done, which is put on gallery view so that you can see everybody.
Right now I'm seeing quite a few of you, and I think everybody that I'm seeing I know and have been in your presence before.
So it reminds me of that.
I'm so grateful that we have online practice.
This pandemic came at the time when we were ready to do what we're doing now.
And there's some great advantages to it, in that we can practice together from a great distance in a way we couldn't before.
So that's an advantage, and maybe it's good that we're not flying around on airplanes and driving around in cars and putting more carbon in the air.
So there's some pretty important advantages, but it is not the same as practicing together face to face.
And who knows whether we'll ever do that again.
But whether or not we do, there's no doubt that we will again, if we are not now to some extent, in the presence of other human beings.
Because that's something we cannot do without.
We are precious to one another.
Being human is needing one another.
In Dharma practice, we bring that sense of human connection to its most basic and most precious point, the point of awakening.
And that's what our story is about.
I remember someone said to me once, "I know your feet."
That's such a funny and intimate thing to say.
From our practicing together in the zendo, barefoot, we know each other's feet.
It's possible to know somebody very well, to have a good friend, but not know their feet.
And yet who are they, if not their feet, their hands, their face, their voice?
They're that more than they are their temporary opinions.
It only takes a moment to know that about someone, a moment in which our minds are quiet and our hearts are wide open.
So it just takes a moment.
But also it takes a really long time, as we know.
Years, decades, in which there are many such moments.
One moment is good, one moment is enough, but also many, many such moments deepens our connection.
Time intensifies our concern and commitment to one another.

One of the greatest experiences you can have in a lifetime, and I hope that we all have had this experience or will have, is the feeling of knowing that there is another person who is really, really for us, really, really with us, no matter what.
And that we know this person, and this person knows us.
And this is not a matter of whether we're going to be with this person all the time, or whether this person is going to be there for us in a time of crisis.
It's something beyond that.
It's an inner knowing that we are here, literally here for and with each other.
And when you have that feeling, you feel really happy and secure, no matter what.
And when you feel it, you don't even need the presence of the other person, because now that presence is within you.
And everywhere you look, you find that person, because you know now that reality is lovely, and it is loving.
And this is not an idea that you have, or a belief that you have, it's a certain feeling inside.
And that maybe takes a little more time.
But I think you feel it little by little.
Despite what people think from the surface, those of us who practice Zen know that Zen is the most tenderhearted, the most other-oriented, the most intimate tradition.
Think about it.
All Zen stories are about sharing life together.
They're always about dialogue and encounter.
In Zen stories, there's no preachings.
There's just sharing words and gestures, as we see in our story.
In Buddhism, we talk about Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
But in Zen, we speak mostly about ancestors.
Ancestors are people who live and die, people that we feel gratitude for and that we take deeply into our lives.
As we take into our lives the presence of our actual biological ancestors, literally we take them into our lives.
We are reorganizations of their DNA, right?
Our body comes from their body.
And in Zen, we understand in just that way.
We join a lineage family, we take in this family's DNA, and it becomes who we are and what we are.
Maybe if I start talking like this, it sounds a little esoteric, a little bit special.
Special Zen intimacy nobody else understands except we Zen people, which is what I used to feel.
How could ordinary people ever understand?
But as time goes on, I can see that this same thing, whether people appreciate it or not, is everywhere you look.
Sometimes it's in families, biological families.
Often it's not, but sometimes it is.
Sometimes you think, how did I have these parents?
I have no idea who these people are.
Other times, there's some very close connection.
I have a lot of friends who are professors training graduate students.
Some of these are Buddhist scholars, some of them are professors of poetry, some of them are scientists.
But in all these cases, they feel a bonding that takes place, a kind of imprinting, a real intimacy between the students and their disciples.
In their case, the basis of the connection is an intellectual tradition, professional.
But in the end, even a professional intellectual tradition becomes more than the ideas that it contains.
The ideas are actually only excuses for deeper feelings of meaning and connection that people in the profession can feel with one another.
Of course, not always, but it happens.
And this sense of intimate connection that we can awaken through our Zen practice could extend to almost any human interaction.
Once we've opened our hearts to it, we can feel it in all encounters, the same kind of connection that's expressed in the story of Long Tan and Tian Huang.
And this is one of the most wonderful virtues of our practice, I think, that it can evoke this sense of closeness everywhere, not just in the Zen community.
In fact, I think this is really important, that we feel this universally and beyond the community.
Because when communities become exclusive and they think they have a special truth that no one outside the community can understand, they become cultish.
And they become very screwed up.
And you can rest assured that the time is coming when people will be hurt by this cultishness.

And when you think about all our great religious traditions, all of which I deeply respect, they all say that their teaching is not exclusive, that the love and compassion that is being cultivated is not just for people in our group.
It's universal.
At least that's what the teachings say, if it's not always true in practice.
That's what's supposed to happen.
Because feelings of exclusivity and the preciousness of our community are very natural and normal.
At our everyday Zen community, half the time we're saying, oh, how wonderful everybody is and how precious the community is, on and on and on.
We love the community.
But when you go too far with that, it's no good.
So the feeling of exclusivity and intimacy within the community is natural and normal and wholesome, but it needs to be extended.
You have to grow out of these feelings for just an exclusive group and extend them to everyone.
So Tian Huang says, "When you greet me, I bow."
As we know, we practice bowing to one another, and it's an old custom from India of showing reverence and respect.
It used to be weird in our culture to do that.
We have the handshake instead, which could seem more intimate than a bow, because we're touching each other.
But now, whoops, not healthy.
Don't shake hands.
Now it's dangerous to shake hands.
A bow is better, because you can do it while you're social distancing, right?
You can social distance and bow to each other.
In bowing, we are acknowledging a friendliness and a respect for each other.
But we're also acknowledging distance, which preserves our health.
When you greet me, I bow.
My bow expresses love and respect for you, but honors the warm space between us that says, I know you are you and I am myself.
I can never assume I understand you.
We meet in the charged, empty space between us, a space full of openness, silence, and not knowing.
Tianhuang said, "When you see it, you just see it.
When you think about it, you miss it."
And then Long Tan has great enlightenment.
It's a simple thing.
It's really not a big deal.
You just see it.
Of course, you can think about it if you want.
And I think it's great fun and very interesting to think about it.
Human beings have minds.
They can think.
It's very fun and interesting to think.
As Dogen teaches us, because Dogen thought about this point, he says, thinking about it, talking about it, writing about it is another form of it.
It isn't about it.
It isn't explaining it.
It is it.
The mind meets a person, a sunset, the sound of a bird, a thought in the mind, a word on the page, and bows.
So this morning I'm talking to you from a distance of 20 or 50 or 1,000 miles or more.
And who knows what I'm saying?
And it doesn't make any difference, really, what I'm saying.
I have been bowing to you.
I have been drinking tea with you.
I have been sitting with you.
I have been practicing this beautiful ritual that we call dharma talk.
And when I'm not talking, I'm listening and talking to you on the phone in Dokusan.
And the best part, the sweetest part for me, is in the beginning when I say, I am bowing to you, and I bow to you, and you bow to me.
That's the best part of the conversation.
I hope all of you in these dramatic times are very well, and that the sesshin is serving you well and supporting your practice.
It's really great for me.

So I hope you will permit me, on behalf of all of us, to dedicate our sesshin from now on as a hope and a prayer for racial justice, and especially, finally, an end to the needless killing of young black men and women.
Among all the things that we pray will be better in the future in our world from now on, today let's pray that we can begin specifically there.
So thank you all very much for your practice, not only in this sesshin, but for many, many years, so many of you, for maintaining the sangha and for listening to my talk today.
Thank you.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.*
*Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
